quote: Wie hat man die Anzahl der willkürlichen Funktionen im allgemeinen Integral zu fassen, wenn man nicht bei der Cauchyschen Potenzreihen- methode stehen bleiben will
english: How should one understand the number of arbitrary functions in the general integral if one does not want to stop at Cauchy's power-series method?
topic: Notes on how to determine general integrals of partial differential equations by boundary data on non-characteristic curves, a conjecture that such solutions depend algebraically on a linearly occurring parameter, and a claim about closed geodesics on closed surfaces illustrated by Finsterwalder's lamella model.

triage.modern_statement: For a system of (possibly nonlinear) PDEs, how can one define and measure, in a way that does not depend on coordinates, how much freedom the general solution has (the 'number of arbitrary functions' of how many variables)? The aim is to do this without just reading the count off the data that the Cauchy power-series method (Cauchy–Kovalevskaya) needs on one particular initial surface, since that count depends on how the problem is set up and does not work for non-analytic data or other ways of specifying data, such as the boundary data on non-characteristic curves discussed on this page.
triage.answered_by: This was never posed as one sharp problem, so it was not 'solved' by one theorem. Instead, a line of later theory answered it. Élie Cartan's theory of exterior differential systems (Cartan–Kähler, early 20th century) introduced the Cartan characters s_i, which measure the arbitrariness of the general solution of an involutive system. Einstein later introduced the 'strength' of a system of field equations, and E. R. Kolchin introduced the differential dimension polynomial in differential algebra. W. M. Seiler (J. Math. Phys. 35, 1994) related Einstein's strength, the Cartan characters and the Hilbert polynomial within the formal (Spencer-type) theory of PDEs. Hilbert himself wrote a related but different paper on ODEs: 'Über den Begriff der Klasse von Differentialgleichungen' (Math. Ann. 73, 1912).

evidence.claim: In Seiler's formal theory, a system is first completed to an involutive one, and then the arbitrariness of the general solution of a q-th order system in n independent variables can be determined (via Cartan characters).

Seiler, 'On the arbitrariness of the general solution of an involutive partial differential equation' (J. Math. Phys. 35, 486, 1994), studies how Einstein's strength, the Cartan characters and the Hilbert polynomial are related, and extends earlier results to nonlinear equations.
Cartan built a sequence of numbers s_i (Cartan numbers or characters) for PDE systems, and these are used to describe the dimension of the solution space.
Kolchin defined the differential dimension polynomial, an invariant that measures the 'size' of a system's solution set in differential algebra.

Hilbert published 'Über den Begriff der Klasse von Differentialgleichungen' in Mathematische Annalen 73 (1912), pp. 95–108. It is a related paper on how general solutions of differential equations can be represented.
Counting degrees of freedom with Cartan characters is still used today, for example for gravity theories.

triage.why: The note is a short, informal question; it is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Its content, though, is the classical question of how to count the 'arbitrary functions' in a general solution in a way that does not depend on coordinates. The standard modern answers are Cartan's characters for involutive systems (Cartan–Kähler), Einstein's strength, Kolchin's differential dimension polynomial, and the formal theory that Seiler shows ties these together. Work in this area continues, for example in degree-of-freedom counting in physics and in differential algebra. Confidence is only medium for three reasons: the note is short; I found no source that links this particular diary entry to these developments; and how directly Hilbert's 1912 paper relates to the PDE question has not been checked.
